## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds. The default recipe gives only 32 PPO updates (131k steps at 4,096 per update) with 4 epochs each, which is very few updates. So the recipe may be blocking learning as much as the architecture. A good placement depends on the landing layer k (the maximum build height under the footprint). Every footprint cell must be in the target at layer k, and the cells between each column's height and k must be empty in the target. The baseline must find this layer indexing on its own using 1x1 convolutions. I test two things. First, a recipe with more updates and fewer epochs on the baseline network. Second, a network with shared weights across layers, which looks at the column relative to each candidate layer k, scores each footprint per k, and combines the k scores with logsumexp. I try that network under two recipes so I can separate the effect of the network from the effect of the recipe.

### Round 2
Every trial so far scored 0 on dev, and training success was also 0, so round 1 gives no signal about which architecture is better. One thing stands out in the recipes. Round 1 changed the recipe in ways that cut the number of gradient steps: the default gives about 4,100 Adam steps, r1c1 gave about 1,800 and r1c3 only about 500. More samples did not make up for that. Getting an exact build needs almost every placement right, so the policy probably needs many more optimiser steps. The new recipe R uses 1 PPO epoch, which gives the most samples. It uses 2,048-sample updates split into 32 minibatches of 64 samples, which gives about 6,000 gradient steps. It also raises lr to 2e-3 and lowers entropy to 0.003 so the policy can sharpen over 257 actions. I test R on the baseline network, on the layer-relative network, and on a deeper layer-relative network. This separates the effect of the recipe from the effect of the network.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success was also 0 in every run. That held across two network families, budgets of 143k to 408k steps, 1 or 2 PPO epochs, and learning rates of 1e-3 and 2e-3. Changing the recipe alone therefore did nothing, and a dense shaped reward should usually give at least a few exact builds. The task warns that this world may differ from its description. Every network so far ties each action logit to the conv feature at the same grid cell and assumes a top-left anchor. If the true mapping from action index to cells differs (for example transposed, mirrored or offset), those networks cannot learn. A head that maps flattened features to all logits through a learned dense layer can learn any mapping. This round tests that with two designs, a pure dense head and a hybrid of the conv head plus a dense head, and also runs the hybrid with a second recipe.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 in training, across very different networks and recipes. These included conv footprint heads, layer-relative heads, dense MLP heads, 1 to 2 PPO epochs, 230k to 425k samples, and short- and long-horizon gamma. Even the 6-brick training designs were never built exactly. Under the stated rules, a conv footprint head can represent an exact building policy, so a total failure points to the world differing from its description. The most damaging difference for conv-aligned heads would be a mismatch between the action index and the cell it acts on: grid transposed, position-major action order, swapped footprints, or a different anchor corner. The dense heads could absorb such a mismatch in principle, but they learn too slowly to show it in this budget. The last round therefore hedges over a set of action-alignment hypotheses, each scored by a learned gain. The action mask, which reflects the true action layout, is fed in as a feature.
